title: IPL Worth $20.6 Billion as Private Equity Reshapes Cricket Business
excerpt: Houlihan Lokey values the IPL at $20.6 billion after a record year of franchise sales and a media-rights boom, as global investors pile into what is becoming sport's most lucrative asset class.
body:
• Houlihan Lokey's 2026 study values the IPL business at $20.6 billion, up 11.4% year-on-year, with the league's standalone brand worth $4.3 billion.
  • Royal Challengers Bengaluru sold for a record $1.78 billion to a consortium including Blackstone; Rajasthan Royals attracted investment at a $1.65 billion valuation.
  • Media rights surged from $918 million in 2008 to $6.2 billion for the 2023-2027 cycle, watched by nearly one billion viewers across television and digital.
  • Top franchises report EBITDA margins of 37-40%, and CVC Capital exited Gujarat Titans with a return above 350% in four years.

The Indian Premier League is now a $20.6 billion business. A Houlihan Lokey valuation of the 2026 season puts the league's business value up 11.4% from last year, with the standalone brand worth $4.3 billion — more than $1.1 billion added since 2023. The number arrives in a year when franchise equity itself shattered records: Royal Challengers Bengaluru changed hands for $1.78 billion, the highest price ever paid for a cricket team, while Rajasthan Royals attracted fresh investment at a $1.65 billion valuation.

The league that launched in 2008 as a brash eight-team experiment is now a financial asset that trades alongside Europe's elite football clubs — and in several valuation metrics, beats them.

The $6.2 billion media-rights engine

Television and streaming contracts did the heavy lifting. The BCCI's media rights for the 2023-2027 cycle fetched $6.2 billion, up from $918 million at the 2008 launch — nearly a sevenfold jump across five rights cycles. A Kotak Mutual Fund report from April puts the full IPL ecosystem at roughly $18 billion as of FY25, nearly matching India's entire sports industry, estimated at about $19 billion.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=rgr13aboaVs

The audience justifies the price. Nearly one billion viewers watched the league across television and digital platforms this year. The 2025 final — RCB's first-ever title win over Punjab Kings at Ahmedabad's Narendra Modi Stadium — drew more than 678 million viewers on JioHotstar alone, surpassing even the India-Pakistan Champions Trophy clash earlier this year. Advertising revenue is projected at around $600 million for 2025, and the league's annual economic contribution is estimated between $182 million and $6.7 billion — up to Rs 62,980 crore, or roughly 0.19% of India's GDP.

The franchise profit machine

Franchises run on one of sport's most favorable revenue splits. The BCCI manages a central pool of about Rs 5,000 crore from media rights and roughly Rs 500 crore from title sponsorships, retaining half and distributing the other half among the teams, according to Storyboard18's breakdown of the league's economics. Clubs layer their own income from sponsorships, gate receipts, and merchandise on top.

Public filings show Chennai Super Kings and RCB generating Rs 500-650 crore in annual revenue with profits of Rs 120-140 crore — EBITDA margins of 37-40% that rank among the highest in global sport. Few teams anywhere combine that margin profile with double-digit annual valuation growth.

From Bollywood owners to Blackstone

What began in 2008 as a league backed by film stars and industrialists has become an institutional asset class. CVC Capital sold its majority stake in Gujarat Titans for a return exceeding 350% over four years. Now KKR, Blackstone, Carlyle, and Partners Group are circling stakes in RCB and Rajasthan Royals at valuations approaching $2 billion.

"Cricket's evolution into a globally owned, institutionally backed asset class has accelerated further in 2026, with the IPL continuing to redefine the global sports landscape."

— Harsh Talikoti, Director, Financial and Valuation Advisory, Houlihan Lokey

The buyer roll tells the story. RCB's record $1.78 billion sale brought together Blackstone, Bolt Ventures, the Aditya Birla Group, and the Times of India Group. Rajasthan Royals drew the Mittal family and Adar Poonawalla. With 1.19 billion viewers, European Business Magazine's analysis describes the IPL as a "scale sports entertainment asset" — driven by predictable cash flows, durable brand equity, and sustained global investor demand.

What's next

Analysts are already marking the next milestone. A published analysis of the league's growth trajectory projects the IPL could reach $25-30 billion in business value by 2030, citing the coming media-rights renewal — likely the league's most competitive auction yet — plus deeper digital monetization and international expansion.

For the Indian diaspora, the numbers land in the living room: the league's nearly one-billion-strong global audience includes a large North American viewership that has made the IPL a prime-time fixture from Edison to Mississauga.
